overview.text: Volume, commonly symbolized V, measures the three-dimensional space occupied by matter or bounded by a surface; unlike area, it is expressed in cubic units. Its SI unit is the cubic meter (m³), while a liter (L) equals a cubic decimeter and a milliliter equals a cubic centimeter, so the same unit system applies to solids, liquids, and gases. In thermodynamics, V describes the space occupied by a system such as a gas: it appears with pressure and temperature in the ideal-gas relation, and a change in gas volume can accompany pressure–volume work. Thus, volume connects everyday measurement with geometry and the analysis of physical systems.

key_facts.text: Volume measures three-dimensional space and is commonly represented by V.
The SI unit is the cubic meter (m³); it can express the volume of a solid, liquid, or gas.
One liter equals one cubic decimeter (1 L = 1 dm³), and one milliliter equals one cubic centimeter (1 mL = 1 cm³).
A cube measuring 10 cm on each side has a volume of 1 L.
For an ideal gas, pressure, volume, and temperature are related; changing a gas’s volume can also involve pressure–volume work.
